query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin, conformal few‐layer graphene coating to tungsten particles before consolidating a W–Cu composite will reduce the thermal resistance at the tungsten–copper interfaces, leading to improved heat flow while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard W–Cu metal-matrix composite with uncoated tungsten particles.
generation.intervention: Coat tungsten particles with a few-layer graphene (or a similarly high-thermal-conductivity 2D material) prior to composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature, cyclic thermal loading and irradiation conditions representative of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The graphene interlayer at the tungsten–copper interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Graphene’s extremely high intrinsic thermal conductivity provides efficient heat transport across the tungsten–copper interface by lowering interfacial resistance, while its robust bonding and ultrathin profile preserve mechanical load transfer and maintain stability under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The graphene-coated composite will exhibit a noticeably higher overall thermal conductivity compared to an otherwise identical W–Cu composite without the coating, without significant losses in mechanical toughness or radiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of a conventional W–Cu composite lacking any interfacial graphene modification.
generation.boundary: The improvement should be observable under operating conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints; however, if the extreme irradiation environment leads to degradation of the graphene layer, the benefit may be reduced.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the thermal conductivity increase is uncertain and may depend on the uniformity and quality of the graphene coating, as well as its behavior under prolonged irradiation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites under identical processing conditions: one using tungsten particles coated with few-layer graphene and one using uncoated tungsten particles. Expose both sets to high temperatures, cyclic thermal loads, and simulated irradiation (e.g., ion irradiation) representative of fusion-reactor conditions.
measurements: Thermal conductivity (e.g., via laser flash analysis)
Mechanical durability (e.g., tensile, creep, and cyclic loading tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-coated composite does not show a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity over the uncoated composite, or if its mechanical durability or irradiation resistance is compromised relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . decision.trend: Earlier research on tungsten‐based and refractory alloys has often concentrated on microstructural tailoring (via processing routes such as directional solidification or advanced powder metallurgy) and interfacial modifications to improve either thermal transport or radiation tolerance. For example, work on tungsten-based high-entropy alloys has demonstrated that controlling phase interfaces and even inducing short-range order can boost thermal conductivity by reducing defect-driven phonon scattering, while other studies have shown that interfacial coatings can enhance bonding and radiation resistance. However, these methods have largely been applied separately – improvements in thermal transport (by adjusting phase architecture or chemical order) have frequently come at the expense of mechanical durability or irradiation stability.
decision.unsolved: The key open problem is to decouple thermal conductivity enhancement from deteriorations in mechanical robustness and radiation resistance. In traditional W–Cu composites, conventional modifications (e.g., altering microstructure or interfacial coatings) tend to improve one property but weaken another, so a single, well-targeted intervention is needed that simultaneously lowers interfacial thermal resistance and preserves the composite’s ability to withstand mechanical loads and radiation-induced damage.
decision.lever: Apply an ultrathin, conformal few-layer graphene (or similarly high-thermal-conductivity 2D material) coating on tungsten particles prior to composite consolidation
decision.why: This intervention leverages graphene’s extraordinarily high intrinsic thermal conductivity and its robust covalent bonding to reduce the thermal resistance at the tungsten–copper interface without compromising the mechanical integrity or irradiation tolerance of the composite. Prior evidence in tungsten-based alloys and related refractory systems shows that interfacial engineering can lead to measurable increases in heat transport while preserving structural stability under extreme conditions. An experiment that prepares two otherwise identical W–Cu composites – one with and one without the graphene interlayer – and then compares their thermal conductivity, mechanical durability (e.g., via creep and tensile testing under cyclic loads), and irradiation resistance (using ion irradiation tests) would be able to falsify or support the hypothesis.
